source_text: Sed licet nulla ex parte constes, tamen quid attuleris prudens lector attendat. Consentiamus voluntatem liberam dici posse, quae bonum velle non potest; hanc autem voluntatem in Baptismate asseris liberari. Interrogo, ad quem modum liberatur? Ut bonum semper velle cogatur, et malum velle non possit? An ut utrumque possit appetere? Hic tu si responderis: Ut bonum semper velle cogatur; quam sis Iovinianista, etiam ipse cognoscis. Si autem dixeris: Quomodo potest esse voluntas libera, si bonum semper velle cogatur? Respondeo: Quomodo dicebatur ante voluntas libera, si malum velle tantummodo cogebatur? Si ergo responderis, sic fieri post Baptisma liberam voluntatem, ut et peccare et non peccare possit; hoc ipso pronuntiabis liberum arbitrium non fuisse, cum utrumque non poterat. Clauderis undique disputationis tuae laqueis; arbitrium ante Baptisma liberum fuit; facultatem habuit faciendi boni, sicut facultatem habuit faciendi mali; et omnis dogmatis tui, quo malum naturale persuades, scena collabitur.
pass_a_gloss: But although you stand from no part, nevertheless let a prudent reader attend what you have brought. Let us consent that a will can be said free, which cannot will good; but this will you assert is freed in Baptism. I ask, unto what manner is it freed? That it be forced always to will good, and cannot will evil? Or that it can seek either? Here if you shall have answered: That it be forced always to will good; how much you are a Jovinianist, even you yourself know. But if you shall have said: How can a will be free, if it is forced always to will good? I answer: How was it being called a free will before, if it was being forced to will evil only? If therefore you shall have answered, that after Baptism a free will is made so, that it can both sin and not sin; by this itself you will pronounce that there was not free choice, when it could not do both. You are shut on all sides by the snares of your disputation; choice before Baptism was free; it had the faculty of doing good, as it had the faculty of doing evil; and the whole scene of your dogma, by which you persuade a natural evil, collapses.

LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: Although you are consistent in no respect, let the sensible reader consider what you have advanced. Let us agree that a will unable to will good can be called free. You assert that this will is freed in baptism. I ask: in what way is it freed? Is it compelled always to will good and unable to will evil? Or can it desire either? If you answer, “It is compelled always to will good”, you yourself recognize how much of a Jovinianist you are. If, however, you say, “How can a will be free if it is compelled always to will good?”, I answer, “How was it called free before, if it was compelled to will only evil?” If you therefore reply that after baptism the will becomes free in the sense that it can both sin and refrain from sin, you thereby declare that there was no free choice when it could not do both. You are enclosed on every side by the snares of your own argument. If choice was free before baptism, it had the capacity to do good just as it had the capacity to do evil; and the whole stage set of your doctrine, by which you urge an evil inherent in nature, collapses.

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
